rationale: A wins because it keeps the story architecture clean: five real lenses, each with a specific desk, a stated weak spot, and proof that would survive a reporter's first callback. A's "Going puts its AI planner behind the paywall — with 2 million free members watching" is a usable business angle; B's "turns a $200 mistake fare into a booked week" invents a fare price and implies booking the product explicitly does not do. B has sharp proof demands, but it lets the headline writer make things up. That is how a decent angle becomes a fact-check problem.
gaps_in_A: "Mistake fares vanish fast" is plausible, but not supplied in the update. Treat it as industry context that needs support, not a given fact.
"If the prevailing push in the space is toward agents that book end-to-end" is properly caveated, but the angle still depends on an external trend not provided here.
"$550 per flight: the savings number Going's paid tier rests on" is useful, but the launch only weakly refreshes that number; A says this, but the angle remains peg-light.
gaps_in_B: "$200 mistake fare" is invented. There is no price in the update, and fake specificity is worse than vagueness.
"into a booked week" is sloppy and misleading. The update says no airline or hotel booking happens in-app.

"the free tier finds the fare, the paid tier tells you what to do with it" overstates the tier mechanics. The facts say Going has free members and a paid Premium/Elite base, not that the free tier gets the same alert flow.
"Two million people get the cheap flight. A fraction of them get the trip." turns member counts into behavior. Two million free members are not two million people getting a specific fare.
